title: Week 18 · Lesson 42: Psychiatric Pharmacology II — Bipolar Disorder, Psychosis, ADHD & Antipsychotic Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 18 — Lesson 42: Psychiatric Pharmacology II — Bipolar Disorder, Psychosis, ADHD & Antipsychotic Safety

FNP-level goal: Use diagnosis-first, safety-first reasoning to recognize bipolar-spectrum illness, psychosis, and ADHD; understand the role and major risks of mood stabilizers, antipsychotics, and ADHD medications; and identify when outpatient management is unsafe.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate mania, psychosis, ADHD symptoms, substance effects, delirium, and medical mimics before selecting medication.
  • Explain the clinical role and key monitoring concerns of lithium, anticonvulsant mood stabilizers, and antipsychotics.
  • Recognize metabolic, movement, cardiac, and rare life-threatening antipsychotic adverse-effect patterns.
  • Apply a careful diagnostic and controlled-substance safety framework to ADHD medication decisions.
  • Recognize red flags requiring emergency evaluation or urgent psychiatric collaboration.

Part 1 — Diagnosis and Safety Come Before the Prescription

Agitation, reduced sleep, distractibility, impulsivity, hallucinations, paranoia, and disorganized behavior are symptoms—not diagnoses. They can arise from bipolar mania, primary psychotic illness, major depression with psychotic features, substance intoxication or withdrawal, delirium, sleep deprivation, thyroid disease, medication effects, neurologic disease, or another medical emergency.

Before changing a psychiatric medication, establish the time course, baseline function, prior episodes, medical history, medications and supplements, substance exposure, sleep pattern, pregnancy potential, and safety status. Assess suicidal or homicidal thoughts, command hallucinations, inability to care for self, severe agitation, violence risk, and access to means. A patient who cannot be kept safe does not belong in a routine outpatient medication workflow.

Part 2 — Mania Is More Than “Feeling Good”

Mania may include elevated or markedly irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased energy, pressured speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity, increased goal-directed activity, impulsive spending or sexual risk, impaired judgment, psychosis, or severe functional disruption. Hypomania can be less impairing but still changes diagnosis and medication planning.

Ask about episodic patterns, family history, prior hospitalizations, and antidepressant-associated activation. New severe mania, psychosis, dangerous impulsivity, inability to sleep for days, or impaired capacity requires urgent assessment. Medication may be part of treatment, but immediate disposition and safety planning come first.

Part 3 — Bipolar Disorder: The Treatment Target Is Mood Stability

Bipolar treatment is not simply “an antidepressant plus something else.” The goal is to address acute mood state, prevent recurrence, preserve function, and reduce self-harm and substance-related risk. Medication selection depends on whether the presentation is mania, depression, mixed features, maintenance care, or an emergency, as well as prior response, comorbidities, pregnancy context, organ function, and specialist recommendations.

When bipolar disorder is suspected, avoid reflexively treating depressive symptoms as uncomplicated unipolar depression. Antidepressant monotherapy can be inappropriate in bipolar-spectrum illness. Coordinate with psychiatry when diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are severe, psychosis is present, or treatment becomes complex.

Part 4 — Lithium: Effective, Useful, and Monitoring-Intensive

Lithium is a mood stabilizer used in selected bipolar-disorder treatment plans. It has a narrow therapeutic index, so safe use requires planned serum-level monitoring and attention to kidney function, thyroid status, hydration, sodium balance, interacting medications, and the individual patient’s clinical status.

Volume depletion, acute illness, major sodium changes, and certain medication interactions can raise lithium exposure and toxicity risk. A patient with new coarse tremor, confusion, unsteady gait, severe GI symptoms, or other concerning neurologic findings while taking lithium needs prompt clinical assessment rather than a casual refill or dose adjustment by message.

Part 5 — Lithium: Connect the Mechanism to the Patient

Think clinically: vomiting, diarrhea, poor oral intake, diuretic use, NSAID exposure, or changes to medications affecting renal blood flow can alter lithium handling. Ask about OTC pain products and every prescriber. Reduced renal clearance is not an abstract laboratory concern—it can turn a previously tolerated regimen into a dangerous one.

Do not give universal dose-change advice in an educational lesson. The FNP task is to recognize risk, obtain timely evaluation and ordered monitoring, use current prescribing information, and coordinate with the clinician managing the mood disorder.

Part 6 — Anticonvulsant Mood Stabilizers

Some antiseizure medications are used as mood stabilizers in bipolar treatment. Each has distinct indications, adverse effects, interactions, reproductive risks, and laboratory or clinical monitoring needs. Do not treat this group as interchangeable.

Valproate-containing therapy requires particular attention to reproductive counseling and patient-specific hepatic, hematologic, pancreatic, and medication-interaction considerations. Lamotrigine is commonly associated with a slow, planned titration strategy because a new significant rash or mucosal/systemic illness can represent a serious reaction. A rash with blistering, mucosal involvement, fever, facial swelling, or systemic illness is urgent—not a routine portal question.

Part 7 — Psychosis: Diagnose the Syndrome, Then Set the Disposition

Psychosis can involve hallucinations, delusions, severe thought disorganization, or markedly impaired reality testing. First determine whether there is immediate danger, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, severe mood illness, infection, metabolic disturbance, or a neurologic cause. An abrupt change in attention or fluctuating consciousness should raise concern for delirium rather than being assumed to be a chronic psychiatric disorder.

New psychosis, command hallucinations, inability to meet basic needs, escalating agitation, or unsafe behavior often requires same-day emergency or specialty evaluation. Primary care coordination is valuable, but it must not delay appropriate crisis care.

Part 8 — Antipsychotics: A Class Requires a Monitoring Plan

Antipsychotic medications may be used for psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, and other evidence-supported indications. They are not interchangeable sleep aids or automatic treatments for nonspecific agitation. Choice depends on diagnosis, acute severity, prior benefit, adverse-effect history, cardiometabolic risk, movement-disorder risk, QT-risk context, other medications, and need for specialty involvement.

Before and during therapy, monitor the patient—not only the symptom score. Document weight/BMI trajectory, blood pressure, glucose or glycemic risk, lipid risk, sedation, orthostasis/falls, movement symptoms, sexual or endocrine effects when relevant, and adherence. The specific monitoring schedule and tests must follow the selected medication’s current labeling and guideline-based plan.

Part 9 — Metabolic Effects: They Matter to Primary Care

Some antipsychotics can contribute to weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, or diabetes. For an FNP, that means psychiatric pharmacology intersects directly with cardiovascular prevention, diabetes care, sleep apnea risk, and patient-centered shared decision-making.

A medication can be clinically necessary and still require active mitigation of cardiometabolic risk. Avoid the false choice between ignoring mental illness and ignoring metabolic health. Coordinate care, assess barriers, and make both outcomes visible in follow-up.

Part 10 — Movement Effects: Learn the Pattern, Not Just the Names

Extrapyramidal symptoms can include acute dystonia, drug-induced parkinsonism, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. Akathisia may feel to the patient like severe inner restlessness and can be mistaken for worsening anxiety or agitation. Tardive symptoms can involve abnormal involuntary movements and need prompt recognition and medication review.

Ask patients and families directly about stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, painful muscle contractions, pacing, inability to sit still, lip-smacking, tongue movements, or other new abnormal movements. Do not dismiss these as “behavioral” without assessment.

Part 11 — Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: A Medical Emergency

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is uncommon but potentially life-threatening. Concerning features can include fever, severe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, and systemic illness in the setting of dopamine-blocking medication exposure. This is an emergency evaluation problem—not an outpatient medication-titration problem.

Clinical urgency matters more than memorizing a single textbook presentation. A systemically ill patient with severe rigidity, fever, confusion, or unstable vital signs needs immediate emergency assessment.

Part 12 — Older Adults, Dementia, and Antipsychotic Risk

Behavioral change in an older adult can reflect pain, infection, dehydration, medication toxicity, constipation, urinary retention, hypoxia, delirium, caregiver stress, or environmental triggers. Assess and treat reversible contributors rather than reflexively adding an antipsychotic.

Antipsychotics carry major safety warnings for elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, including increased mortality risk. Use must be individualized, indication-based, and coordinated with the patient, caregivers, and appropriate specialists—not used as a convenience intervention.

Part 13 — ADHD: Confirm the Developmental Pattern

Adult patients often present with “poor focus,” but ADHD diagnosis requires more than current distraction. Obtain a developmental history, evidence of symptoms across settings, functional impairment, and assessment for anxiety, depression, trauma, sleep disorders, substance use, bipolar disorder, medication effects, and learning issues. A rushed diagnosis can lead to the wrong medication and missed underlying disease.

For children and adolescents, gather age-appropriate history from caregivers, school, and the patient; assess impairment in more than one setting; and use validated tools as adjuncts rather than replacements for clinical assessment.

Part 14 — Stimulants: Benefit With Controlled-Substance Responsibility

Stimulant medications can be effective for appropriately diagnosed ADHD, but they require careful baseline assessment and follow-up. Review cardiovascular history, blood pressure, pulse, sleep, appetite/weight, tics or movement history, psychiatric symptoms, substance-use risk, diversion risk, other sympathomimetics, and the state-specific controlled-substance requirements that govern practice.

Medication monitoring includes function: Is attention improving? Is school/work performance safer and more consistent? Are sleep, appetite, mood, and vital signs acceptable? Is the medication being taken only as prescribed? A refill interval alone is not meaningful ADHD follow-up.

Part 15 — ADHD and Bipolar/Psychosis Risk

Stimulant-associated activation, worsening mania, or psychotic symptoms requires immediate reassessment of diagnosis, safety, medication exposure, substance use, and disposition. Do not assume that a patient becoming sleepless, grandiose, paranoid, or severely agitated merely needs a different stimulant dose.

When ADHD coexists with bipolar disorder, psychosis, significant anxiety, cardiovascular disease, or substance-use disorder, treatment planning often benefits from psychiatric and interprofessional collaboration.

Part 16 — Clinical Case: “Depression” With Escalating Risk

A 26-year-old started an antidepressant two weeks ago and now reports sleeping two hours nightly, rapid speech, impulsive online purchases, irritability, and feeling “unstoppably productive.”

FNP reasoning: this pattern suggests possible activation or unrecognized bipolar-spectrum illness. Assess for mania, psychosis, substance exposure, suicidality, and ability to stay safe. Do not simply renew the medication or advise waiting for the adverse effects to pass; arrange urgent evaluation and psychiatric support as indicated.

Part 17 — Clinical Case: Restlessness Is Not Always Anxiety

A patient recently started an antipsychotic and says, “I feel like I have to keep moving. I cannot sit through dinner.” They have no prior history of this symptom.

FNP reasoning: consider akathisia and review the full medication timeline, severity, safety, and other movement symptoms. Calling this “worsening anxiety” without examining the medication relationship can prolong distress and lead to inappropriate treatment escalation.

Part 18 — Clinical Case: ADHD Request With a Different Diagnosis

A 34-year-old requests a stimulant for poor concentration. Further history reveals loud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, escalating alcohol use, and a recent job loss.

FNP reasoning: impaired concentration may be secondary to sleep-disordered breathing, substance use, depression, or another condition. Complete a focused diagnostic and safety assessment before assigning an ADHD diagnosis or prescribing a controlled stimulant.

FNP Psychiatric Pharmacology II Framework

  1. Identify the syndrome and rule out immediate medical, substance-related, or delirium causes.
  2. Assess safety: suicide, violence, command hallucinations, grave disability, severe mania, and capacity to follow an outpatient plan.
  3. Match treatment to the diagnosis and phase of illness; do not use a symptom label as the diagnosis.
  4. For mood stabilizers and antipsychotics, build the laboratory, interaction, movement, metabolic, and reproductive-safety plan before follow-up is due.
  5. For ADHD medications, confirm developmental impairment and assess cardiovascular, psychiatric, sleep, misuse, and diversion risk.
  6. Escalate urgently for severe mania, psychosis with unsafe behavior, possible medication emergency, or inability to maintain safety.

High-Yield Summary

Bipolar disorder: ask about mania/hypomania before treating depression as unipolar illness.
Lithium: requires planned monitoring; dehydration, kidney clearance, sodium changes, and interactions can create toxicity risk.
Antipsychotics: require metabolic, movement, orthostatic/sedation, cardiac-risk, and indication-based monitoring.
NMS pattern: fever + rigidity + altered mental status + autonomic instability is an emergency.
ADHD: diagnosis requires a developmental, multi-setting impairment pattern—not today’s distractibility alone.
Stimulants: require controlled-substance, vital-sign, sleep, psychiatric, misuse, and diversion safeguards.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Psychiatric diagnosis, psychotropic medication selection, dosing, serum-level interpretation, tapering, controlled-substance management, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, FDA-approved prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
